transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-11-05
Start: 15:30 PST
Duration: 46 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Carlos Mendes (Acme Head of ML), Ellen Park (Acme SRE), Ravi Kumar (Acme Eng Mgr)

[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh this is Jordan from Redwood, i'm the AE on the account, with me is priya our solutions engineer. quick roll call?
[00:10] Carlos: hey carlos here, hi all.
[00:12] Ellen: ellen on SRE.
[00:14] Ravi: ravi here.
[00:16] Priya: great, thanks. the goal for today is to scope the POC and specifically nail down the benchmark plan and how you'll integrate your scripts into our harness. is that right jordan?
[00:26] Jordan: yup, and clarify success criteria and timelines.
[00:28] Carlos: absolutely, we want to validate both performance and cost for our most common workloads. main concerns are streaming chat flows and non-streaming batch summarization jobs.
[00:38] [00:40] Priya: ok great — can you describe the workload mix and expected QPS? like what's steady state QPS, and what bursts look like?
[00:46] Carlos: steady is pretty low, around 5 rps for the chat front-end but bursts can go to 50 rps during peak events. batch summarization jobs are async — roughly 200 requests every 10 minutes, but those are larger tokens.
[00:58] Ravi: to add, p95 latency requirement for interactive chat for us is about 300ms, p99 ideally under 600ms. if latency spikes we drop to fallback model which reduces quality.
[01:12] Priya: that helps. for the POC we usually run two phases: a functional correctness/quality phase with your prompts, and a performance phase where we replay traffic with your representative scripts. for the harness we support locust and k6 out of the box, and also a simple node/python client if you prefer.
[01:30] Carlos: we have an existing load harness that exercises our dialogue system. can we just plug that in? it's a Node script that streams tokens and measures latency.
[01:38] Priya: yes, but streaming adds complexity for metrics. streaming sessions keep connections open and you need to measure time-to-first-token, time-to-last-token, and sustained throughput. our harness has a streaming adapter you can call, but you'll need to map your socket events to our expected metrics.
[01:54] Ellen: what's the overhead of streaming in terms of cost? do we pay per token same as non-streaming?
[01:59] Jordan: cost model is token-based for both; small overhead may exist for open connections but tokens are the main driver. Priya can show the exact telemetry fields we collect.
[02:08] Priya: yeah we emit token counts, total tokens, and per-request latency histograms. we also collect kv-cache hit rates for certain workloads where we do prefix caching. note sometimes transcriptions of our product names get munged — people say 'Redwood Dedicate' instead of 'Redwood Dedicated' in notes, just FYI.
[02:26] Carlos: haha, got it. for quality metrics, we want to run an eval set of ~500 prompts. we also want automatic diffing between outputs to check regressions vs our baseline model. can the harness support that?
[02:36] Priya: yes, we can run a deterministic eval (non-streaming) and compute ROUGE/BLEU or embedding similarity. for chat style streaming we capture final output after stream completes and then run the quality checks.
[02:48] Ravi: how do we simulate token length distribution? our batch jobs often hit 8k tokens.
[02:54] Priya: we can parametrize the harness with token-length histograms; for long sequences we recommend running a separate heavy-IO lane to avoid smoothing out the latency of interactive requests. also include sequence length as a tag so we can break out metrics by bucket.
[03:08] [03:12] Jordan: timeline — team expects a 2-week POC: week one integration and functional tests, week two full benchmarks and results. is that feasible for you?
[03:20] Carlos: yes two weeks sounds right but we need the harness template early so our engs can wire it into our CI.
[03:25] Priya: i'll share a repo with example locust scenarios, a streaming adapter and a node script for your existing harness. we'll also include a sample k6 script if you use that.
[03:34] Ellen: on networking — we plan to do VPC peering for the Dedicated instance. what do you need from us?
[03:40] Priya: we'll need IP ranges, peering window and the list of ports. also ensure any egress rules allow outbound to our control plane for telemetry. for Private/on-prem we have an extra checklist but for peering it's usually IPs and an ACL.
[03:52] Carlos: is there an option to avoid peering and use a public endpoint with mTLS? our security team prefers not to open peering for now.
[03:58] Jordan: yes, if you can't peer we can do a public endpoint + mTLS and IP allowlist, but there are throughput differences sometimes. peering gives lower latency and more predictable egress.
[04:08] Ravi: ok noted. what about data retention and logs — we need audit logs and any PII should not persist on Redwood.
[04:14] Priya: we support customer-managed keys and can configure no-persist for request bodies in the POC; audit logs are available for enterprise tiers. we'll include the security pack doc in the follow-up.
[04:24] Carlos: for benchmarks, what metrics do you usually report back?
[04:28] Priya: we produce p50/p90/p95/p99 latency, time-to-first-token for streaming, throughput (req/s), tokens/s, error rates, and cost per 1k tokens and cost per effective request. we also surface tail latencies and CPU/GPU utilization if we run Dedicated.
[04:44] Ellen: will you run the POC on our dedicated pool or on hosted?
[04:48] Jordan: for the pilot we can spin up a small Dedicated pool to match your production target, otherwise we also run an initial smoke test on hosted to validate the harness quickly. Dedicated requires a short provisioning lead time.
[04:58] Carlos: provisioning lead time — how long?
[05:00] Jordan: usually 3-5 business days for a small Dedicated slice, depending on region, but we can do hosted within a day to validate scripts.
[05:10] [05:12] Priya: one gotcha with streaming load tests — common tools like locust open many sockets which triggers connection limits. we usually recommend a hybrid approach: use locust for non-streaming replay and a scaled streaming runner that reuses connections, or a custom harness that simulates multiplexed streams.
[05:28] Ravi: our node script already reuses connections; we'll adapt it to send the same messages and measure first-token latency. is there an example mapping?
[05:36] Priya: yes, i'll attach an example mapping in the repo: event -> ttf, complete -> ttf-last, token-count event-> aggregate. we also recommend instrumenting with client-side timestamps and server-side telemetry alignment.
[05:50] Carlos: about success criteria — beyond latencies we need quality parity within a 5% embedding similarity vs our baseline and cost within 20% of current spend. can those be part of the acceptance matrix?
[06:02] Jordan: absolutely, we'll include a success criteria table in the SOW: latency SLOs, quality thresholds, cost targets, and regression tolerances.
[06:10] Ellen: who will own the benchmark runs? we'd prefer Redwood to run the first pass and then we'll run a mirrored run in our environment.
[06:16] Priya: that works. Redwood will run the initial harness against a Dedicated/hosted endpoint, collect telemetry, then we handover the harness and configs so you can run in your environment. sync on results and triage regressions together.
[06:28] Carlos: fine. can you show us the sample dashboard we give at the end?
[06:32] Priya: quick share — (describes) the dashboard breaks out latency by model version, by token-length bucket, cost per thousand tokens, and streaming-first-token distribution. we'll share a sample PDF with typical charts.
[06:44] Ravi: ok good. small question — for batch 8k token jobs, do you recommend quantization or a specific model variant?
[06:52] Priya: for long sequences we often recommend a quantized variant for Dedicated; it reduces memory and cost. we'll recommend per-workload model/quantization profile in the POC report. note quantization can slightly affect quality so we'll include eval checks.
[07:06] Carlos: perf testing — do you simulate cold starts and KV cache warmups?
[07:10] Priya: yes, we run both cold-start runs and warm runs with KV cache primed. we also do continuous batching tests to observe throughput gains. include both in the plan.
[07:20] Jordan: okay let's capture next steps and owners.
[07:24] (brief cross-talk)
[07:30] Carlos: one more security item: we need SOC 2 attestation and a list of sub-processors for legal.
[07:36] Jordan: we'll attach SOC 2 + ISO docs and a sub-processor list in the follow up.
[07:40] Ellen: timeline recap?
[07:43] Jordan: we'll share SOW and harness repo by Friday (2025-11-07). you provide dataset and peering window by next Monday/Tuesday. week one integration, week two benchmark runs, and final report within 48 hours of tests.
[07:56] Carlos: sounds good.
[07:58] Priya: i'll also include examples for the streaming adapter and a short how-to doc on measuring ttf and token counts.
[08:06] Ravi: about reporting — will the cost numbers include GPU costs? we want a breakdown by model config (fp16 vs int8) and per-request cost.
[08:14] Priya: yes, we'll report cost per config including GPU-hour estimates and token-based cost. for Dedicated we show estimated committed vs on-demand delta.
[08:24] Ellen: ok let's stop there and we'll follow up on the action items. thanks everyone.
[08:29] Jordan: thanks all, we'll send notes and artifacts. bye.

Post-meeting notes: some transcription errors around product names and acronyms, e.g., 'kv cache' transcribed consistently but sometimes 'Redwood Dedicated' appeared as 'Redwood Dedicate'. references to tools: locust spelled correctly, k6 sometimes seen as 'k six' in speech.

Referenced artifacts/links:
- Redwood POC SOW template (link sent post-call)
- Benchmark harness repo (will be shared): examples/locust-streaming-adapter.js, examples/k6-nonstream.js
- Security pack PDF (SOC2, ISO, sub-processors)

End of transcript.
